Transfer Appliance is for offline scenarios where network bandwidth is severely limited. Dataflow adds unnecessary complexity for a bulk file copy.

questions.q: A data team stores 500 TB of raw JSON log files in Cloud Storage. The data is accessed daily for the first 30 days, then accessed once a month for 6 months, then rarely accessed after that. What lifecycle policy minimizes cost while maintaining data availability?
choices: Keep all data in Standard storage to ensure immediate availability when accessed infrequently
Transition objects to Nearline after 30 days, then to Coldline after 90 days, then to Archive after 365 days
Set a lifecycle rule to delete all objects after 30 days to eliminate storage costs entirely
Move all objects to Nearline immediately on upload to reduce storage costs from the start
questions.explanation: Cloud Storage lifecycle management can automatically transition objects to lower-cost storage classes based on age. Moving to Nearline (minimum 30-day retention, $0.01/GB) after 30 days, to Coldline (90-day minimum, $0.004/GB) after 90 days, and to Archive (365-day minimum, $0.0012/GB) after 1 year matches the access pattern while minimizing cost. Deleting after 30 days loses the data. Standard storage is unnecessarily expensive for rarely accessed data. Moving to Nearline on upload incurs retrieval fees for the first 30 days of frequent access.

questions.q: A company is migrating a MySQL database with 5 TB of data to Cloud SQL. The migration must be online (zero downtime) with minimal impact to the production MySQL server. After cutover, the Cloud SQL instance should be in sync with the final transactions. Which migration tool supports this pattern?
choices: Use Database Migration Service (DMS) with continuous replication to sync changes from MySQL to Cloud SQL until cutover

Configure Cloud SQL External Server Replication to make Cloud SQL a replica of the on-premises MySQL database and sync changes to BigQuery — External Server Replication replicates to Cloud SQL but does not sync changes directly to BigQuery; a separate migration step to BigQuery is still required

Use mysqldump to export the entire database, copy to Cloud Storage, then import into Cloud SQL — mysqldump creates a full snapshot without continuous sync or ongoing replication; a separate cutover step would still require downtime to apply changes accumulated since the export

Deploy Datastream from the on-premises MySQL source to Cloud SQL using binlog-based CDC for near-real-time migration sync — Datastream targets BigQuery, Cloud Storage, or Cloud Spanner as destinations; it does not natively stream binlog-based CDC changes from MySQL directly into Cloud SQL
questions.explanation: Database Migration Service (DMS) performs an initial full dump migration followed by continuous CDC (change data capture) using MySQL binlog replication. During the replication phase, the source production server continues serving traffic while DMS keeps Cloud SQL in near-real-time sync. At cutover, the application is pointed to Cloud SQL. This achieves minimal downtime and minimizes impact on the source server. mysqldump requires a maintenance window for cutover. Datastream can replicate to BigQuery but is not designed to write to Cloud SQL. External Server Replication (Cloud SQL as a read replica of an external MySQL) is similar to DMS but DMS provides a managed UI, monitoring, and promotion workflow.

questions.q: A financial services company stores customer transaction records in Cloud Spanner. Queries frequently join a `transactions` table with an `accounts` table on `account_id`. The team wants to minimize cross-node RPC calls for this join. Which Spanner design feature should they use?
choices: Shard both accounts and transactions tables manually by hashing account_id across multiple databases — manual sharding duplicates application complexity and does not leverage Cloud Spanner's native interleaving, which co-locates rows for the same accounts on the same server

Use commit timestamps on the transactions table to enforce time-ordering of writes for accounts that share an account_id — commit timestamps impose serialization overhead and do not reduce cross-server joins between accounts and their transactions
Interleave the `transactions` table inside the `accounts` table using `account_id`

Create a secondary index on account_id in both tables to speed up the join between accounts and transactions — secondary indexes improve lookup speed but do not physically co-locate accounts and transaction rows, so the join still crosses server boundaries
questions.explanation: Interleaved tables in Cloud Spanner co-locate child rows with their parent row in the same Spanner split, eliminating cross-node RPCs for parent-child joins. Transactions interleaved inside accounts on `account_id` means all transactions for an account are stored adjacent to that account row. Secondary indexes speed lookups but do not eliminate cross-node joins. Manual sharding is managed by Spanner automatically. Commit timestamps track change order but do not affect co-location.

questions.q: A team maintains a Cloud Spanner database for a global inventory management system. They need to detect all rows modified in the last 10 minutes for a real-time audit log without polling the database. Which Spanner feature enables this?
choices: Enable Spanner Change Streams on the target tables and consume change events via the Dataflow Spanner Change Streams connector
Query the `information_schema.SPANNER_STATISTICS` view periodically to detect rows with recent `LAST_MODIFIED` timestamps
Use Datastream to replicate Spanner CDC events to BigQuery and query the BigQuery audit table
Configure a Spanner commit timestamp column and poll for rows where `last_modified > CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE`
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner Change Streams capture DML changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) at the partition level and expose them as a stream. The official Dataflow Spanner Change Streams connector reads this stream in real time and can route changes to BigQuery, Pub/Sub, or other sinks without polling. `information_schema.SPANNER_STATISTICS` does not provide row-level change events. Datastream does not currently support Spanner as a source (it supports MySQL and PostgreSQL). Polling a commit timestamp column requires write-side schema changes and introduces polling latency.

questions.q: A company is designing a Cloud Spanner schema for a multi-tenant SaaS application. Each tenant has millions of user records. Queries frequently filter by `tenant_id` and sort results by `created_at` descending to show recent users. Which schema design best supports this query pattern while preventing hot spots?
choices: Use a primary key of `(tenant_id, created_at DESC, user_id)` so rows are physically co-located by tenant and sorted by recency
Use a primary key of `(GENERATE_UUID(), tenant_id)` to randomize row distribution and add a secondary index on tenant_id
Use a primary key of `(tenant_id, user_id)` and add a commit timestamp column `created_at ALLOW_COMMIT_TIMESTAMP` for tracking
Use a primary key of `(user_id)` with a secondary index on `(tenant_id, created_at DESC)` for filtered, sorted lookups
questions.explanation: Using `(tenant_id, user_id)` as the primary key co-locates all rows for a tenant in the same key range, making tenant-scoped queries efficient without cross-split reads. Adding a `created_at` column with `ALLOW_COMMIT_TIMESTAMP` automatically records the server-side write timestamp, enabling time-ordered queries. Monotonically increasing `created_at DESC` in the primary key can cause write hot spots in Spanner because all new rows for a tenant land at the same split boundary. A secondary index can cover the sorted-by-recency query efficiently. UUID prefix randomizes distribution but requires a secondary index for tenant filtering.

questions.q: A data platform team wants to enforce data quality rules across raw and curated zones of their Cloud Storage-based data lake — including schema validation, null checks, and referential integrity — with results visible in a central governance UI. Which GCP service best addresses this requirement?
choices: Configure BigQuery data policies and column-level security tags to enforce quality standards — controls access rather than producing data quality results
Build a Cloud Composer DAG that runs custom Python validation scripts and writes results to a shared BigQuery audit table for governance review
Use Dataplex data quality tasks with YAML-based rule definitions, surfacing results in the Dataplex console with pass/fail metrics per rule
Apply Cloud DLP inspection jobs over each zone and surface results in the DLP dashboard — detects sensitive data, not schema or null-check quality results
questions.explanation: Dataplex provides native data quality tasks that run on BigQuery tables and GCS data assets. Rules are defined in YAML (row completeness, column nullability, referential checks) and results appear in the Dataplex console with pass/fail metrics. Cloud DLP is for sensitive data discovery, not schema or null validation. Cloud Composer DAGs can do validation but require custom code and lack a built-in governance UI. BigQuery data policies control access, not quality.

questions.q: A data engineering team uses Dataplex to organize their Cloud Storage data lake. They want to automatically discover, catalog, and apply data quality checks to all Parquet files landing in the `raw` zone. What is the correct Dataplex setup?
choices: Configure Dataplex Catalog to crawl the raw storage zone bucket and apply quality checks via a custom Cloud Function triggered on new files — Dataplex Catalog discovers metadata but custom Cloud Functions are not the native way to apply zone-level data quality rules within a Dataplex lake

Write a Cloud Composer DAG that runs Great Expectations checks on all new Parquet files in the raw storage zone and sends alerts on failure — this approach adds data quality checks but does not register metadata in a Dataplex lake or enforce quality rules as part of the lake zone governance framework

Use BigQuery external tables pointing to the Dataplex-managed raw Parquet files in the storage zone and run BigQuery Data Quality rules — BigQuery external tables can query the files but do not integrate with Dataplex lake quality policies applied at the zone level
Create a Dataplex lake with a `raw` zone, attach the Cloud Storage bucket as a managed asset with auto-discovery enabled, and create Dataplex data quality tasks for the discovered Parquet tables
questions.explanation: Dataplex provides an integrated data lake management platform. Creating a Dataplex lake and raw zone, then attaching the Cloud Storage bucket as an asset with auto-discovery enabled, causes Dataplex to automatically scan new Parquet files, infer schemas, register them in the metadata catalog, and make them available for Dataplex data quality tasks. This is the native, end-to-end workflow. Data Catalog can crawl GCS but does not natively run quality checks. Cloud Composer with Great Expectations is a valid but custom solution requiring code maintenance. BigQuery external tables with scheduled queries lack auto-discovery and the unified governance UI that Dataplex provides. attach the Cloud Storage bucket as a Dataplex asset with auto-discovery enabled, and create data quality tasks for the discovered tables
